Part 1 of 6

The Youth Revolt

CORE OBJECTIVE

Core Objective 1: Explore the origins of the youth revolt, and compare the responses of the New Left and the counterculture.

IN MY WORDS: Young people in the 1960s rebelled in two ways. What were the two groups, and how were they different?

Reading AThe New Left

As criticism of U.S. combat involvement in Vietnam mounted, idealistic but increasingly disillusioned young people flowed into two overlapping yet distinct movements: the New Left and the counterculture.

The political arm of the youth revolt originated in 1960 with the formation of Students for a Democratic Society (SDS). . . . Their goal was ambitious: to quit reading history and start making history by transforming the United States into a more democratic society.

At the gathering, Tom Hayden, a veteran of the civil rights struggle in the South, drafted an impassioned document known as the Port Huron Statement. . . . Within a few years, more than 1,000 campuses were hosting SDS chapters, and the organization began publishing an underground newspaper, The Rag.

Word help: disillusioned = let down, no longer trusting · impassioned = full of strong feeling · chapters = local groups of a club

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 28, “‘Forever Young’: The Youth Revolt” (The New Left) (p. 1261).

Reading BThe Draft and Anti-War Protests

The Vietnam War was primarily a poor man’s fight. Most college students were able to postpone military service until they received their degree or reached the age of twenty-four. . . . African Americans and Latinos were twice as likely to be drafted as Whites.

As the war dragged on, opposition to U.S. involvement exploded. Some 200,000 young men ignored their draft notices, and some 4,000 served prison sentences for doing so. . . . Others defied the draft by burning their draft cards while shouting “Hell, no, we won’t go!”

Word help: drafted = forced by law to join the military · postpone = put off until later · defied = refused to obey · draft cards = papers men had to carry showing they could be drafted

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 28, “‘Forever Young’: The Youth Revolt” (Anti-War Protests) (p. 1262).

A poor man’s fight. Reading B says the Vietnam War “was primarily a poor man’s fight.” Give two facts from the reading that show who was most likely to be drafted.

Reading CThe Counterculture

Hayden acknowledged that the shocking events of 1968 led those who came to be known as hippies to embrace the counterculture—an unorganized and leaderless rebellion that focused more on personal exploration and the pursuit of authenticity, however one defined it, than on political activism.

Both the counterculture and the New Left rejected the status quo, but most hippies preferred to “drop out” of mainstream society rather than mobilize to change the political system. The change that they sought was organic, growing out of the alternative communities they created. Self-exploration and self-expression were their goals, not taking over campuses and shutting down government offices. “Make Love, Not War” became their motto.

The countercultural rebels were primarily middle-class Whites alienated by the Vietnam War, racism, political corruption, and parental authority. . . . They chose another path to the good life by embracing the outlook popularized by former Harvard clinical psychology professor Timothy Leary: “Turn on, tune in, drop out.”

Word help: Hayden = Tom Hayden, a founder of SDS · hippies = young people in the counterculture · authenticity = being real or true to yourself · status quo = the way things are now · mobilize = organize people to act · alienated = feeling left out or turned off

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 28, “‘Forever Young’: The Youth Revolt” (The Counterculture) (p. 1265).

Part 2 of 6

Social Activism Spreads

CORE OBJECTIVE

Core Objective 2: Assess the influence of the youth revolt and the civil rights movement of the early 1960s on other protest movements, and how new protest movements affected social attitudes and public policy.

IN MY WORDS: Which earlier movement inspired women, Latinos, Indigenous Americans, and gay and lesbian Americans to protest? Name one law or court case they won.

Reading DThe Women’s Movement

The civil rights movement inspired women, Latinos, Native Americans, gay men and lesbians, the elderly, and people with physical and mental disabilities to demand equal opportunities and equal rights.

In 1966, Friedan and other activists founded the National Organization for Women (NOW). . . . The new organization sought to end gender discrimination in the workplace and spearheaded efforts to legalize abortion and obtain federal and state support for child-care centers.

A major victory came in 1972, when Congress approved an equal-rights amendment (ERA) to the U.S. Constitution. . . . By 1982, the ERA had died, being three states short of ratification.

Title IX of the Educational Amendments of 1972 barred gender discrimination in any “education program or activity receiving federal financial assistance.”

Word help: Friedan = Betty Friedan, a writer · discrimination = unfair treatment · amendment = a change added to the Constitution · ratification = official approval by the states · federal financial assistance = money from the national government

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 28, “Social Activism Spreads” (Betty Friedan; Equal Rights Amendment; Fractured Feminism; Title IX) (pp. 1272–1278).

Reading ERoe v. Wade (1973)

In 1973, in Roe v. Wade the justices ruled 7–2 that states must allow women, married or single, to have abortions before the twelfth week of pregnancy. . . . However, the Court’s controversial decision, and the ensuing success of NOW’s efforts to liberalize local and state abortion laws, generated a powerful conservative backlash, especially among Roman Catholics and evangelical Protestants, who mounted a powerful “right-to-life” crusade that helped fuel the conservative political resurgence in the 1970s and thereafter.

Word help: ensuing = following · liberalize = make less strict · backlash = a strong reaction against something · crusade = a big campaign · resurgence = coming back stronger

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 28, “Social Activism Spreads” (Roe v. Wade) (p. 1277).

Picture 1What Women Want

Norton prints these two photographs side by side. Left: the Women’s Strike for Peace and Equality marches down Fifth Avenue in New York City in August 1970. Right: eight years later, Phyllis Schlafly leads a much smaller group at the Illinois State Capitol to protest the Equal Rights Amendment (ERA). (Both are primary sources.)

What to look for: Strike = a protest where people stop work · Sisterhood = women standing together · Stop ERA = against the Equal Rights Amendment · a crushing blow = a terrible hit

Norton, Ch. 28, “Social Activism Spreads,” Visual Explorations: “What Women Want” (p. 1278). Primary sources (photographs, 1970 and 1978).

Picture 1. (1) Read the signs. What did the marchers on the left want? (2) What did the protesters on the right want? (3) Which side won the fight over the ERA (Reading D)?

Reading FFarmworkers and Students

By 1965, Chavez and Dolores Huerta, a former teacher, had converted the Farm Workers’ Association into the UFW. . . . Over the next ten years, Chavez and Huerta led nonviolent protest marches, staged hunger strikes, and managed nationwide boycotts. . . . Finally, in 1970, the grape growers agreed to raise wages, offer health benefits, and improve working conditions.

The United Farm Workers was a rural civil rights movement, but in 1968 the struggle for more rights expanded into urban areas as well. . . . The students were protesting the poor conditions of their school buildings, overcrowded classrooms, high dropout rates, a shortage of qualified teachers, and the district’s emphasis on vocational training rather than college preparation.

Word help: UFW = United Farm Workers, a union for farmworkers · Chavez = Cesar Chavez, a Mexican American labor leader · boycotts = refusing to buy something as a protest · rural = in the country, on farms · The students = some 22,000 mostly Mexican American students who walked out of East Los Angeles schools in March 1968 · vocational = job training

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 28, “Social Activism Spreads” (Cesar Chavez and the United Farm Workers; Chicano Students and the “Blowouts”) (pp. 1279–1281).

Reading GRed Power

Indigenous peoples also emerged as a political force in the late 1960s. The federal reservation policy dating to the nineteenth century, along with continuing racism and discrimination, created miserable conditions in many Indigenous communities.

On November 20, 1969, fourteen Red Power activists occupied Alcatraz Island, in San Francisco Bay. Over the next several months, hundreds of others, mostly students, joined them.

In 1968, the year before the Alcatraz occupation, George Mitchell and Dennis Banks, two Chippewas (or Ojibwas) living in Minneapolis, founded the American Indian Movement (AIM). . . . In 1973, AIM led 200 Sioux protesters in occupying the tiny South Dakota village of Wounded Knee, where in 1890 the U.S. Seventh Cavalry had massacred an entire Sioux village.

Word help: reservation = land set aside by the government for a tribe · occupied = took over a place and stayed · massacred = killed many people

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 28, “Social Activism Spreads” (Indigenous Americans’ Quest for Equality; The American Indian Movement) (pp. 1283–1284).

Reading HThe Stonewall Uprising (1969)

Then an event occurred that mobilized the gay and lesbian population to action. At 3 A.M. on June 28, 1969, a New York City Police Department vice squad raided the Stonewall Inn, the most popular gay/transgender club in Greenwich Village. There had been raids before, but this time the police were determined to shut down the Stonewall Inn—for good.

The Stonewall Uprising was a turning point in the movement for gay rights. Although there had been many protests and demonstrations before, the Stonewall riots crystallized the quest for gay legitimacy. . . . and it helped many others to see the gay/lesbian/trans liberation movement as interwoven with the struggle for civil rights.

Word help: mobilized = got people ready to act · vice squad = police who arrested people for breaking moral laws · uprising = a rebellion · crystallized = made clear and strong · legitimacy = being accepted as normal and legal

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 28, “Social Activism Spreads” (Stonewall) (pp. 1285–1286).

Part 3 of 6

Nixon and the Silent Majority

CORE OBJECTIVE

Core Objective 3: Analyze how Richard Nixon's election strategy and domestic policies were affected by the political environment of the late 1960s.

IN MY WORDS: Who were the voters Nixon tried to win, and what were they angry about?

Reading IThe “Silent Majority”

The turmoil of the 1960s spawned a cultural backlash among what President Richard Nixon called the “great silent majority” of middle-class Americans who had propelled him to victory in 1968. He had been elected as the representative of middle America—that is, voters fed up with student radicals, hippies, radical feminism, gay and lesbian rights, and programs of affirmative action that gave preferential treatment to people of color and women to make up for past injustices.

Nixon promised to restore “law and order” by “cracking down” on anti-war protesters, civil rights demonstrators, and activists who challenged traditional gender roles.

Word help: turmoil = confusion and disorder · backlash = a strong reaction against something · propelled = pushed · affirmative action = programs that gave extra chances to people of color and women · preferential treatment = special treatment

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 28, “Nixon and the Revival of Conservatism” (The Conservative Backlash; “Law and Order”) (pp. 1288–1289).

Reading JThe Sun Belt and the Southern Strategy

A major reason for Nixon’s election victories in 1968 and 1972 was his ability to win votes in the South. Civil rights laws had transformed the region, creating enduring resentments among many White voters.

By the 1970s, the former Confederacy was being included in what commentators referred to as “the Sun Belt.” This new term encompassed the states stretching across the southern United States from the Carolinas to southern California, the most economically dynamic states in the nation. . . . The population boom brought the Sun Belt states of the South, the Southwest, and California more congressional seats, more electoral votes, and more political power (see Map 28.1).

In the 1972 election, Nixon easily carried every southern state. . . . Yet even more explicitly than he had four years earlier, Nixon pursued a “southern strategy” that capitalized on White resentments of federal civil rights laws.

Word help: resentments = angry feelings about being treated unfairly · Confederacy = the southern states that left the Union in 1861 · economically dynamic = growing fast in jobs and money · explicitly = openly · capitalized on = used to his advantage

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 28, “Nixon and the Revival of Conservatism” (Nixon and the Sun Belt) (pp. 1290–1291).

MapMap 28.1: The Rise of the Sun Belt

This modern textbook map shows which states gained and lost people in the 1970s. The shaded curve marks the Sun Belt across the South and Southwest.

Map key: Orange = states with population gain · Blue = states with population loss · Shaded curve = the Sun Belt · + number = people gained · − number = people lost

Norton, Ch. 28, Map 28.1, “The Rise of the Sun Belt” (p. 1291). Modern textbook map.

Map evidence. (1) Name two states that gained many people. (2) Name two states that lost people. (3) Use Reading J: why did a growing Sun Belt help Nixon and the Republicans?

Reading KNixon at Home: The Environment and the Economy

Nixon knew that if he vetoed legislative efforts to improve environmental quality the Democratic majorities in Congress would overrule him, so he chose not to stand in the way. . . . In 1970, Nixon signed the Clean Air Act and an executive order that created two federal agencies, the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).

The major domestic development during the Nixon administration was a floundering economy. The accumulated expense of the Vietnam War and the Great Society programs helped quadruple the annual inflation rate from 3 percent in 1967 to 12 percent in 1974. . . . Economists coined the term stagflation to describe the simultaneous problems of stalled economic growth (stagnation), rising inflation, and high unemployment.

Word help: vetoed = refused to sign a law · executive order = an order from the president · inflation = rising prices · unemployment = people without jobs · floundering = struggling · stagnation = an economy that stops growing

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 28, “Nixon and the Revival of Conservatism” (Nixon and Environmental Protection; “Stagflation”) (p. 1294).

Part 4 of 6

Ending the War and Easing the Cold War

CORE OBJECTIVES

Core Objective 4: Analyze how and why Richard Nixon and Henry Kissinger changed military and political strategies to end America's involvement in the Vietnam War.

Core Objective 5: Examine Nixon's and Kissinger's global foreign policy strategy during the 1970s and what they hoped it would accomplish.

IN MY WORDS: How did Nixon get U.S. troops out of Vietnam, and how did he try to get along better with China and the Soviet Union?

Reading L“Peace with Honor” and Vietnamization

Privately, he had decided by 1969 that “there’s no way to win the war,” so he sought what he and Kissinger called “peace with honor.” That is, the United States needed to withdraw from the war in a way that upheld the credibility of its military alliances around the world.

On the second front, Nixon tried to defuse the anti-war movement. To do so, he steadily reduced the number of U.S. troops in Vietnam to enable what he called the Vietnamization of the war—that is, the equipping and training of South Vietnamese soldiers and pilots to assume the primary burden of combat. From a peak of 560,000 U.S. troops in 1969, only 50,000 remained in Vietnam by 1973. . . . in 1973 as his program of Vietnamization progressed, the president ended the draft altogether by creating an all-volunteer military.

Word help: he = President Nixon · credibility = being believed and trusted · alliances = partners who promise to help each other · defuse = calm down · burden = heavy load · all-volunteer military = no one is drafted

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 28, “‘Peace with Honor’: Ending the Vietnam War” (Gradual Withdrawal) (p. 1296).

Reading MKent State and the End of the War

In the spring of 1970, news of the secret Cambodian “incursion” by U.S. forces set off explosive protests on college campuses and in cities across the nation. In Ohio, the governor sent the National Guard to Kent State University to control campus rioting. But in a shocking turn of events, the poorly trained guardsmen panicked and opened fire on rock-throwing demonstrators, killing four student bystanders.

Between the time Nixon took office in 1969 and the signing of the Paris Peace Accords in 1973, another 20,000 U.S. troops had died in Vietnam; military morale had been shattered; and millions of Southeast Asians had been killed, wounded, or displaced. Worst of all, fighting soon broke out again in both Vietnam and Cambodia.

On April 30, 1975, Americans watched on television as North Vietnamese tanks rolled into Saigon, soon to be renamed Ho Chi Minh City, and military helicopters airlifted U.S. embassy and South Vietnamese officials and their families to warships offshore.

Word help: incursion = a sudden attack into another country · National Guard = a state’s part-time soldiers · bystanders = people who were just watching · morale = spirit and confidence · displaced = forced from their homes · airlifted = carried away by aircraft

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 28, “‘Peace with Honor’: Ending the Vietnam War” (Kent State and Jackson State; War without End; The Collapse of South Vietnam) (pp. 1298–1300).

Reading NThe Nixon Doctrine and Détente

Their grand design for U.S. foreign policy after the Vietnam War centered on developing friendly relations with the Soviet Union and Communist China while using the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) to intervene in the politics of less developed nations.

Under the Nixon Doctrine, the United States would support proxy warfare by providing weapons and money—but not American troops—to other governments or groups to fend off Communist insurgencies.

At the same time, Nixon announced that he would pursue partnerships with Communist countries in areas of mutual interest. That Nixon, with his history of unwavering anti-communism, would embrace such a policy of détente (a French word meaning “easing of relations”) shocked many observers and demonstrated yet again his pragmatic flexibility.

Word help: Their = Nixon’s and Kissinger’s · intervene = get involved · proxy warfare = helping others fight instead of sending your own troops · insurgencies = armed rebellions · détente = easing of tensions · pragmatic = practical

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 28, “The Nixon Doctrine and a Thawing Cold War” (The Nixon Doctrine) (pp. 1301–1302).

Reading OChina, the Soviet Union, and SALT I

In February 1972, during “the week that changed the world,” Nixon arrived in Beijing. Americans watched on television as the president shook hands and drank toasts with Prime Minister Zhou Enlai and Communist Party chairman Mao Zedong.

Nixon and Brezhnev signed the pathbreaking Strategic Arms Limitation Treaty (SALT I), which negotiators had been working on since 1969. The agreement did not end the nuclear arms race, but it did limit the number of missiles with nuclear warheads and prohibited the construction of missile-defense systems.

Word help: Beijing = the capital of China · Brezhnev = the leader of the Soviet Union · pathbreaking = the first of its kind · warheads = the explosive part of a missile

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 28, “The Nixon Doctrine and a Thawing Cold War” (The People’s Republic of China; Embracing the Soviet Union) (pp. 1303–1304).

Part 5 of 6

Watergate

CORE OBJECTIVE

Core Objective 6: Explain how the Watergate scandal unfolded and assess its political significance.

IN MY WORDS: What was Watergate, and how did it end?

Reading PThe Break-In and the Cover-Up

On June 17, 1972, police in Washington, D.C., captured five burglars breaking into the Democratic National Committee headquarters in the sprawling Watergate hotel-apartment-office complex. The burglars were caught installing illegal listening devices on phones in the Democratic Party offices.

When the news of the burglary broke, Nixon and his staff denied any involvement, dismissing the incident as a “third-rate burglary.” But the president was lying. He told Alexander Haig, then his national security adviser, that “we will cover up [the Watergate burglary] until hell freezes over.” Thus began the scandal commonly referred to as Watergate.

Word help: burglars = people who break in to steal · listening devices = hidden microphones (“bugs”) · cover up = hide the truth

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 28, “Watergate and Its Aftermath” (The Nixon Administration and “Dirty Tricks”) (p. 1307).

Reading QThe Tapes, Impeachment, and Resignation

In July 1974, the Supreme Court ruled unanimously that the president must surrender all the Oval Office tape recordings. A few days later, the House Judiciary Committee voted to recommend three articles of impeachment against Nixon: obstruction of justice through the payment of hush money to witnesses and the withholding of evidence; abuse of power through the use of federal agencies to deprive citizens of their constitutional rights; and defiance of Congress by withholding the tapes.

Nixon finally gave up. On August 9, 1974, he resigned from office, the only president to do so.

In 1973 and 1974, Congress passed several pieces of legislation designed to curb executive power. . . . Congress passed the War Powers Act (1973) over President Nixon’s veto. It requires the president to inform Congress within forty-eight hours if U.S. troops are deployed in combat abroad and to withdraw them after sixty days unless Congress specifically approves their stay or passes a declaration of war.

Word help: unanimously = all the judges agreed · impeachment = charging a president with crimes so he can be removed · obstruction of justice = blocking an investigation · hush money = money paid to keep people quiet · curb = limit

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 28, “Watergate and Its Aftermath” (Growing Desperation; Watergate and the Presidency) (pp. 1309–1310).

Source RPresident Ford Speaks to the Nation (Primary Source)

Gerald Ford became president on August 9, 1974, the day Nixon resigned. Ford had never been elected president or vice president. He said these words in a televised address that day.

“I am acutely aware that you have not elected me as your President by your ballots . . . So I ask you to confirm me as your President with your prayers. . . . our long national nightmare [Watergate] is over. Our Constitution works; our great Republic is a government of laws and not of men.”

Word help: acutely aware = know very well · ballots = votes · confirm = accept, approve · nightmare = a very bad dream · Republic = a nation governed by elected leaders · a government of laws and not of men = the law is above any one person

Gerald R. Ford, televised address, August 9, 1974. Quoted in Norton, Ch. 28, “Watergate and Its Aftermath” (Gerald Ford: An Unelected President) (p. 1311).

Source R. Ford says, “Our Constitution works.” What happened in Watergate that shows the system worked? Use Reading Q.

Point of view. Ford had not been elected. Why would he want to tell Americans that the “nightmare” was over? What did he hope people would feel?
